nE: Roll Ball Side Lying Scalene Muscles Activation
nR: Активация лестничных лёжа на боку мячом
nH: הפעלת סקלנים בשכיבה צדדית עם כדור
t: Place a rollball on an exercise mat and lie on your side, keeping your body in a straight line from head to hips. | Stack your knees and bend them slightly for stability; rest your bottom arm extended along the floor or use it to lightly support your head. | Lift your head and slide the rollball beneath the lateral side of your neck, positioning it roughly midway between your ear and the top of your shoulder. | Lower your head gently onto the ball so its weight alone provides the pressure — do not push down actively. | Breathe slowly and allow the scalene muscles to soften under the sustained contact for 20–30 seconds. | Make small adjustments — tilt your chin slightly toward the ceiling or let it drop toward your chest — to shift pressure across the anterior, middle, and posterior scalene fibers. | When you find a tender spot, hold steady and breathe through the discomfort until it softens, typically 20–45 seconds. | Reposition the ball slightly higher or lower along the lateral neck to address additional areas of tightness. | To finish, support your head with your top hand, lift it clear of the ball, then roll onto your back and rest for a moment before repeating on the opposite side.

Breathe deeply and allow the tissue to soften rather than bracing against the discomfort. | While holding on a tender area, slowly raise and lower your arm overhead or perform small shoulder blade rolls to dynamically change the tension angle and deepen the release. | Adjust the pressure by shifting more or less weight through your feet — adding load by extending your legs slightly, or reducing it by pressing more firmly through your feet. | Work through one side for 60–90 seconds, then carefully remove the ball, reposition it to the other side of the spine, and repeat the sequence on the opposite lower trapezius.

t: Place the rollball on a firm surface or hold it in your hand, and position yourself so you can press the ball against your upper trapezius — the area between the top of your shoulder and the base of your neck. | You can perform this seated, standing against a wall, or lying on your side, whichever allows you to control the pressure comfortably. | Slowly roll the ball along the upper trapezius from the base of your neck toward the top of your shoulder, pausing whenever you find a tender spot. | When you locate a tight area, hold the ball still on that point and maintain moderate pressure for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily. | Relax the muscle as much as possible while the ball holds pressure — avoid tensing the shoulder upward. | After the hold, gently tilt your head away from the side being worked to increase the stretch through the upper trapezius. | Continue rolling slowly along the muscle, repeating the pause-and-hold at each tender point. | Work the full length of the upper trapezius, then switch sides and repeat the process.

t: Place a foam roller on the floor and lie face-down with your body fully extended. | Position the roller under one upper arm, just below the shoulder, with your palm facing the floor. | Extend the working arm out to the side at roughly a 45–90° angle from your torso so the biceps rests directly on top of the roller. | Support your body weight on your opposite forearm and the toes of both feet. | Slowly roll the foam roller down your upper arm from just below the shoulder toward the crease of the elbow, using gentle pressure. | Pause for 2–3 seconds on any tight or tender spot, maintaining steady pressure without forcing through sharp pain. | Continue rolling back up toward the shoulder, working the full length of the biceps brachii. | Complete 30–60 seconds on one arm, then switch to the other side.

t: Sit on the floor with your legs extended in front of you and place a foam roller under both calves, just above the Achilles tendon. | Put your hands on the floor behind your hips and press down to lift your glutes off the ground, transferring your body weight onto the roller. | Cross one ankle over the other to stack weight on a single calf and increase pressure. | Slowly roll toward your knee until the roller reaches just below the back of the knee, then reverse the motion back toward the ankle. | When you find a tender or tight spot, pause on it for 20–30 seconds and let the tissue relax before continuing. | After completing one leg, switch by uncrossing your ankles, cross the opposite ankle on top, and repeat on the other calf. | Work each calf for 60–90 seconds, targeting both the center of the muscle (gastrocnemius) and the sides to reach the soleus underneath. | Finish by gently flexing and pointing your foot a few times to encourage blood flow through the released tissue.

t: Sit on the floor with your legs extended in front of you and place the foam roller under your right calf, just above the Achilles tendon. | Cross your left ankle over your right shin to stack your body weight onto the right leg. | Place your hands flat on the floor behind your hips and press down to lift your glutes off the ground. | Slowly roll forward along the calf until the roller reaches just below the back of your knee, then reverse the direction. | Move at a steady, controlled pace — roughly one to two seconds in each direction — rather than rolling quickly. | When you find a tender or tight spot, pause on it for two to three seconds and let the pressure release before continuing. | After completing the full length of the calf, rotate your leg slightly inward and then outward to expose the inner and outer portions of the gastrocnemius and soleus. | Finish the set, then switch legs by placing the roller under your left calf and crossing your right ankle over for the same sequence.

t: Place a foam roller on the floor horizontally. | Lie face down and position the roller under your chest, just below your collarbone, with your arms extended forward or out to the sides for support. | Support most of your weight on your forearms or hands and lightly brace your core so your lower back does not sag. | Slowly shift your body forward so the roller moves down toward the middle of your chest, then shift back to move it toward the upper chest. | When you reach a tender spot, pause for 20–30 seconds and breathe deeply to let the tissue relax before continuing. | Continue rolling at a slow, even pace across the full width of your chest, spending extra time on tight areas. | To target one side more specifically, tilt your body slightly to that side and shift your weight onto the corresponding pectoral. | After 30–60 seconds of rolling, or once the tissue feels less restricted, gently press up with your arms and lift yourself off the roller.

t: Place a foam roller on the floor and sit at one end of it with your knees bent and feet flat. | Slowly lower yourself backward so the roller runs lengthwise along your entire spine, from tailbone to the base of your skull. | Keep your knees bent and feet flat on the floor to stabilise your lower body throughout the stretch. | Let your arms fall out to the sides with palms facing up, positioning them between 45° and 90° relative to your torso — find the angle where you feel the most tension across your chest. | Allow gravity to draw your chest open and your shoulders toward the floor, breathing steadily and without forcing the stretch. | Hold the position for 30–60 seconds, taking slow, deep breaths to encourage progressive relaxation of the chest and anterior shoulders. | To finish, bring your arms back to your sides, roll to one side, and use your hands to press yourself back up to seated.

nR: Прокатка разгибателей спины лёжа на полу

t: Place a foam roller horizontally on the floor. Sit on the floor in front of it with your knees bent and feet flat. | Lean back and position the foam roller just below your shoulder blades, supporting your upper body with your hands behind your head or crossed over your chest. | Lift your hips off the floor so your body weight shifts onto the roller and your feet. | Using your feet to control movement, slowly roll the foam roller down toward your lower back, targeting the erector spinae on either side of the spine. | Pause on any tender or tight spot for 20–30 seconds, breathing deeply to allow the tissue to release. | Continue rolling slowly down until the roller reaches the top of your hips, stopping before it reaches the tailbone. | Roll back up toward the shoulder blades at the same controlled pace, working the full length of the paraspinal muscles. | Repeat the pass 2–3 times, spending extra time on areas that feel particularly tight. | To finish, lower your hips to the floor, remove the roller, and rest for a moment with your knees pulled gently to your chest.

t: Place the foam roller horizontally on the floor and sit in front of it with your knees bent and feet flat. | Carefully lower yourself so the roller sits at the base of your skull, cradling the back of your head — not the middle of your neck. | Allow your head to rest fully on the roller and let your arms relax at your sides, palms facing up. | Take a slow, deep breath in and, on the exhale, consciously release tension through your neck and shoulders. | Gently tilt your chin slightly toward your chest to elongate the back of the neck, then return to neutral — do not force the movement. | Slowly roll the foam roller a centimetre or two downward so it contacts the upper cervical spine just below the skull; pause and breathe for 20–30 seconds. | Continue inching the roller down in small increments along the cervical spine, pausing at any tender spot until the tension eases. | Stop rolling before the roller reaches the base of your neck at the shoulders; avoid placing direct pressure on the lower cervical vertebrae. | To finish, place both hands behind your head for support, lift your head off the roller, and roll to one side before pressing yourself back up to seated.

t: Sit on a mat with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hands resting lightly on your shins. | Tuck your chin gently toward your chest and round your lower back to initiate the roll. | Use a controlled, smooth motion to roll backward, vertebra by vertebra, until your shoulder blades contact the mat — do not roll onto the back of your neck. | As you reach the bottom of the roll, keep your legs together and begin to draw them back over your torso if performing a full rollover, or let them rise naturally as you reverse direction. | Engage your core and reverse the momentum, pressing through the lower back and hips to begin rising back up. | As your torso lifts, extend your legs out in front of you at roughly a 45-degree angle, keeping them straight and together. | Find your balance point on the tailbone, lifting your chest tall and extending your arms forward or to the sides for stability — this is the V-sit. | Hold the V-sit for one to two seconds, keeping the core braced and the legs straight. | Lower your feet back to the mat with control and immediately flow into the next repetition.

nE: Roll Peroneal Side Lying on Floor
nR: Прокатка малоберцовых лёжа на боку на полу

nR: Прокатка грудного отдела лёжа на полу
nH: גלגול עמוד שדרה חזי בשכיבה על הרצפה עם רולר
t: Place the foam roller on the floor perpendicular to your body's long axis. | Sit on the floor in front of the roller, then lower your upper back onto it so the roller sits just below your shoulder blades (roughly the T7–T8 level). | Interlace your fingers behind your head to support your neck, and bring your elbows slightly forward so they frame your face. | Plant your feet hip-width apart on the floor and lift your hips a few centimetres off the ground to load weight onto the roller. | Inhale to prepare, then exhale and gently let your upper back extend over the roller, allowing gravity to open the thoracic segment beneath it. Hold for 1–2 seconds. | Press through your feet to slowly shift your hips forward, rolling the foam roller 2–3 cm up your spine toward your upper back. nR: Прокатка передней большеберцовой на одной ноге лёжа на полу

t: Lie face down on the floor and place the foam roller perpendicular to your lower leg, positioning it just below the knee on the upper shin. | Extend the working leg fully and rest the opposite leg on the floor beside it, or cross it over the working leg to add more pressure. | Prop yourself up on your forearms, keeping your core lightly engaged and your upper body relaxed. | Shift enough body weight onto the roller so you feel moderate pressure along the tibialis anterior — the muscle running beside the shinbone. | Slowly roll down the shin toward the ankle in a controlled 2–3 second stroke, keeping the movement smooth and deliberate. | Roll back up toward the knee with the same slow pace, covering the full length of the muscle belly. | When you reach a tender or tight spot, pause and hold steady pressure on that area for 20–30 seconds until you feel the tension release. | Continue rolling up and down for 30–60 seconds total on the working leg. | Lower that leg to the floor, switch sides, and repeat the full sequence on the other leg.

t: Lie flat on your back with legs extended and feet together. Reach both arms straight overhead close to your ears, pressing your lower back gently into the floor. | Inhale to prepare, drawing your navel gently toward your spine to engage your core. | Exhale as you float your arms toward the ceiling and begin to curl your head and shoulders off the floor, leading with the crown of your head rather than your chin. | Continue exhaling as you peel your spine off the floor one vertebra at a time, rolling through your mid-back and then lower back in a slow, sequential wave. | Reach your arms forward toward your feet and fold at the hips into a seated forward bend, keeping your spine as long as possible. | Hold the stretched position for one breath, feeling the lengthening through your lower back and waist. | Inhale, then exhale as you begin rolling back down by tilting your pelvis posteriorly and lowering your lumbar spine to the floor vertebra by vertebra. | Continue lowering through your mid-back, upper back, and finally your head, returning your arms overhead to the starting position. | Rest briefly, then repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining the same slow, controlled tempo in both directions.

t: Set the Roman chair so the foot rollers sit just above your ankles when you are seated, allowing your legs to be nearly straight or slightly bent. | Sit on the pad and hook your feet under the foot rollers, pressing the tops of your feet firmly against them. | Cross your arms over your chest or place your hands lightly behind your head without interlacing your fingers. | Inhale and slowly lower your torso backward, allowing your lower back to extend past horizontal toward the floor — go only as far as your flexibility and strength allow. | Pause briefly at the bottom without losing tension in your core. | Exhale and contract your rectus abdominis to curl your torso back up toward your thighs. | At the top, squeeze your abs for one count before beginning the next rep. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining a controlled tempo on both the lowering and lifting phases.

t: Adjust the Roman chair so the thigh pad sits just above your hips, allowing your torso to hang freely below horizontal. Set the ankle pads to grip your heels securely. | Step up and position yourself face-up on the apparatus, hooking your feet under the ankle pads and resting the tops of your thighs against the thigh pad. | Cross your arms over your chest or hold them straight alongside your torso to keep your upper body neutral. | Brace your core lightly and lower your torso back in a controlled arc until it drops slightly below the horizontal line of your hips. Do not let gravity pull you down uncontrolled. | Pause briefly at the bottom, feeling a stretch through the front of your hips. | Contract your hip flexors to drive your torso back up, rising until it is roughly parallel to the floor or slightly above. | Hold the top position for a brief moment before beginning the next controlled descent. | After completing your target reps, step down from the apparatus carefully.

t: Stand at the base of the rope and reach up as high as you can with both hands, gripping firmly with your thumbs wrapped around the rope so it sits across the base of your palms. | Pull your body up by driving your elbows toward your hips, initiating the movement with your lats and back rather than curling with your arms alone. | As you rise, bring your knees up and wrap the rope around one foot — pass it on the outside of one shin, then step on it with the opposite foot to lock it in place. | Stand up through your legs to push yourself higher, then immediately reach up with both hands to a new grip position above the previous one. | Continue alternating between a foot-lock push and a hand-over-hand pull to ascend the rope one segment at a time. | At the top, briefly control your position before beginning the descent — do not release suddenly. | Descend by easing the foot lock and lowering your hands in controlled segments, using your grip to brake rather than sliding freely. | Return to the floor under control and rest fully before your next climb.

t: Start in a high push-up position with your hands directly under your shoulders, arms fully extended, and your body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and keep your feet hip-width apart so your whole body stays rigid throughout the movement. | Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows, keeping them at roughly a 45° angle to your torso. | Press explosively back up until both arms are fully extended. | Rotate your torso to one side, lifting one arm off the floor and reaching it straight toward the ceiling so your body forms a T-shape. | Hold the top position for one to two seconds, keeping your hips level and your raised arm fully extended. | Return the raised hand to the floor under control and reset to the starting push-up position. | Perform the next rep and rotate to the opposite side, alternating arms each repetition.

t: Start on your hands and knees with your hands placed slightly wider than shoulder-width apart and your knees on the floor directly below your hips. | Walk your hands forward until your body forms a straight line from your knees to the top of your head, keeping your core braced and hips level. | Lower your chest toward the floor in a controlled push-up, keeping your elbows at roughly a 45-degree angle from your torso. | Press back up to the starting position, fully extending your arms. | As you complete the press, shift your weight onto your left hand and rotate your torso to the right, lifting your right arm toward the ceiling. | Stack your right hip on top of your left and hold the side position briefly, keeping your core tight and your body in a straight line from knees to head. | Lower your right arm back to the floor and return to the starting push-up position with both hands on the ground. | Perform the next push-up and rotate to the opposite side, lifting your left arm toward the ceiling. | Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions.

t: Lie face down on a mat with your legs extended and your hands placed flat beside your shoulders, fingers pointing forward. | Press through your hands to lift your chest and torso off the mat, straightening your arms as far as your flexibility comfortably allows while keeping your hips in contact with the floor — this is your starting position. | Take a slow breath in to lengthen and decompress your spine. | Exhale and gently rotate your torso to the right, looking over your right shoulder until you feel a stretch along the left side of your abdomen and obliques. | Hold the rotated position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily without forcing the range. | Return your gaze forward and bring your torso back to center with control. | Rotate to the left, looking over your left shoulder, and hold for the same duration. | Lower yourself back to the mat and repeat for the desired number of sets.

t: Stand with your feet together and your arms at your sides, facing forward with a tall, upright posture. | Jump your feet out to shoulder-width or slightly wider, landing softly on the balls of your feet with a slight bend in the knees. | As your feet land wide, swing both arms up and simultaneously rotate your torso to the right, letting your hips follow naturally. | Jump your feet back together and return your arms to your sides, squaring your torso back to center on the landing. | On the next jump out, rotate your torso to the left with the arm swing, mirroring the movement from the other side. | Continue alternating the rotation direction with each rep, maintaining a steady, controlled rhythm throughout. | To finish, complete your final rep, land with feet together, and come to a controlled standing stop.

t: Stand with your feet hip-width apart or position yourself prone over a stable surface such as a bench edge so your hips are at the pivot point. | Let your spine curl forward into a fully rounded position — tuck your chin toward your chest and allow your lower back to flex gently. | With your hands resting lightly behind your head or extended in front of you, brace your core just enough to maintain control. | Begin the movement by initiating from your hips: squeeze your glutes and drive your hips forward as you start to lift your torso. | Continue extending until your spine reaches a neutral, straight alignment — avoid hyperextending the lower back at the top. | Hold the extended position for one count, feeling the engagement through the hip extensor region and lower back. | Slowly reverse the motion by re-rounding your spine from the top down, returning to the fully flexed starting position under control. | Complete all reps with a smooth, deliberate tempo, keeping each phase of the movement controlled rather than momentum-driven.

t: Stand in your fighting stance with feet shoulder-width apart, dominant foot back, hands raised in guard position at chin level. | Shift your weight onto your front (non-kicking) foot and begin to pivot on the ball of that foot, rotating your hips toward the target. | As you pivot, lift your rear knee up and out to the side so the thigh is roughly parallel to the floor — this is your chamber position. | Drive your shin and foot outward and forward in a horizontal arc, snapping through the target zone with the shin or instep. | Keep your standing leg slightly bent throughout to maintain balance and absorb the rotational force. | Hold your guard hand up on the kicking side to protect your face during the delivery. | After contact, retract your kicking leg back through the same arc rather than dropping it straight down. | Return your foot to your fighting stance and reset your guard before continuing.

t: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and feet flat. Place your hands behind your thighs and sit tall with your spine long. | Lean back slightly until your core engages, then lift your feet off the floor so your shins are parallel to the ground — this is the half-boat starting position. | Release your hands and extend your arms forward at shoulder height, palms facing each other and fingers pointing toward your feet. | Inhale as you extend your legs out to roughly a 45-degree angle and sweep your arms overhead, lengthening through the spine. | Exhale and draw your knees back toward your chest, simultaneously sweeping your arms forward and down in a rowing arc — as if pulling oars through water. | Continue the rhythm — inhale to extend legs and reach arms overhead, exhale to draw in knees and pull arms forward — for the desired number of repetitions. | To finish, lower your feet to the floor on an exhale, sit upright, and release the core engagement.

t: Sit on the rowing machine seat and secure your feet in the foot straps, positioning the strap across the widest part of your foot. | Grip the handle with both hands using an overhand grip, keeping your wrists flat and relaxed. | Start in the catch position: knees bent, shins vertical, arms straight, and torso leaning slightly forward from the hips — not the lower back. | Initiate the drive by pressing through your heels to extend your legs powerfully. | Once your legs are nearly straight, swing your torso back just past vertical — roughly 10–15 degrees of layback — by hinging at the hips. | Draw the handle in toward your lower ribs by pulling your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades together. | Pause briefly at the finish position with legs extended, torso leaning back slightly, and the handle at your lower ribs. | Reverse the sequence for the recovery: extend your arms forward first, hinge your torso forward, then bend your knees to glide back to the catch position. | Maintain a smooth, controlled rhythm throughout and breathe out on the drive and in on the recovery.

t: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides, and your gaze forward. | Begin jogging in place, lifting your knees to roughly hip height and landing softly on the balls of your feet. | After 4–8 running steps, plant both feet shoulder-width apart and pause briefly to set your base. | Hinge slightly at the hips and bend your knees to roughly 45° — a half squat — keeping your chest up and back flat. | Hold the half-squat position for one count, ensuring your knees track over your second toe and your weight stays through your full foot. | Press through your heels to stand fully upright, then immediately transition back into the running-in-place phase. | Continue alternating between the running and half-squat phases continuously for the prescribed duration or rep count. | Breathe rhythmically throughout — inhale as you lower into the squat and exhale as you drive back up.

tHe: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides, and your gaze forward. | התחל לרוץ במקום, הרם את הברכיים בערך לגובה האגן ונחת ברכות על כריות כפות הרגליים. | אחרי 4–8 צעדי ריצה, נטע את שתי הרגליים ברוחב הכתפיים ועצור לרגע לייצוב הבסיס. | Hinge slightly at the hips and bend your knees to roughly 45° — a half squat — keeping your chest up and back flat. | Hold the half-squat position for one count, ensuring your knees track over your second toe and your weight stays through your full foot. | Press through your heels to stand fully upright, then immediately transition back into the running-in-place phase. | Continue alternating between the running and half-squat phases continuously for the prescribed duration or rep count. | נשיר בקצב קבוע לאורך כל התרגיל — נשאב בעת הירידה לסקוואט ונשיר בעת ההנעה חזרה למעלה.

t: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and arms relaxed at your sides. | Begin running in place, lifting your knees to roughly hip height and swinging your arms naturally in opposition to your legs. | After two to four running steps, push off the balls of both feet to hop upward, driving your arms forward or overhead for momentum. | Land softly on the balls of your feet with your knees slightly bent to absorb the impact. | Immediately transition back into the running-in-place rhythm without pausing. | Maintain an upright torso and relaxed shoulders throughout — avoid hunching forward. | Continue for the prescribed time or rep count, then slow to a walking march to bring your heart rate down.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, arms at your sides, and core lightly braced. | Begin running in place by lifting your knees toward hip height in a quick, alternating pattern, pumping your arms in opposition as you would when jogging. | After the designated number of steps or seconds, plant both feet and prepare to transition to the jumping jack phase. | Jump your feet out to roughly shoulder-width while simultaneously raising both arms out and overhead in a wide arc. | Without pausing, jump your feet back together and bring your arms back down to your sides to complete one jumping jack. | Immediately return to running in place to begin the next repetition of the drill. | Keep alternating between running in place and jumping jack jumps for the full set duration, aiming for a continuous, rhythmic pace. | Breathe steadily throughout — inhale through your nose and exhale through your mouth — and avoid holding your breath between phases.

t: Stand upright with feet hip-width apart and arms relaxed at your sides. | Run in place or over a short distance for 3–5 quick steps, pumping your arms naturally. | Plant both feet simultaneously, landing with a soft bend in the knees. | Lower into a partial squat by pushing your hips back and bending your knees to roughly 45 degrees — thighs should not yet be parallel to the floor. | Drive through your heels and mid-foot, extend your hips and knees, and jump vertically. | Swing your arms upward to generate momentum as you leave the ground. | Land on the balls of your feet first, then lower your heels, absorbing impact through bent knees and hips. | Immediately transition back into the running phase and repeat the sequence for the target number of reps or time.

t: Step onto the treadmill and place both feet on the side rails before starting the machine. | Set your target speed — begin at a comfortable walking pace (3–4 mph) and increase gradually to your intended running speed. | Step onto the moving belt and walk briefly to establish your balance and stride rhythm before accelerating. | Accelerate to your running pace, aiming for a midfoot strike that lands beneath your center of mass rather than far out in front of your heel. | Maintain an upright torso with a slight forward lean originating from the ankles, not the waist; keep your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears. | Drive your elbows back at roughly 90° and swing your arms naturally in line with your direction of travel — do not let them cross the midline of your body. | Breathe rhythmically — inhale for two to three strides and exhale for two to three strides — to sustain effort and manage pace. | At the end of your session, reduce speed gradually to a walking pace and complete 2–3 minutes of cool-down walking before stopping. | Step off to the side rails before the belt comes to a full stop, or wait for it to stop completely before dismounting.

t: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and feet flat. Lean back slightly until you feel your core engage, keeping your spine long and neutral rather than rounded. | Lift your feet a few inches off the floor to increase the challenge, or keep them grounded if you are new to the exercise. | Extend both arms straight out in front of you and clasp your hands together with fingers interlaced. | Rotate your torso to the right while simultaneously driving your clasped hands down in a diagonal chopping motion toward your right hip. | Pause briefly at the bottom of the chop, feeling the contraction in your right oblique. | Reverse the motion by sweeping your arms up and across your body to the left side, rotating your torso with them. | Drive your hands down in a diagonal chop toward your left hip, keeping your hips as square and stable as possible. | Continue alternating sides in a controlled, fluid motion for the desired number of repetitions on each side.

nE: Russian Twist (on stability ball arms straight)
nH: פיתולים רוסיים (על כדור פיזיו בידיים ישרות)
t: Sit on the stability ball with your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. | Walk your feet forward until the ball sits under your upper back and shoulders, forming a tabletop position with your hips at roughly the same height as your knees. | Brace your core so your body holds a straight line from knees to shoulders, and keep your feet planted about shoulder-width apart for a stable base. | Extend your arms straight above your chest, clasp your hands together, and keep your elbows locked throughout the movement. | Rotate your torso slowly to the right, letting your shoulders roll across the ball and your arms follow, while keeping your hips level and your arms fully extended. | Pause briefly when your torso is as far right as your range of motion allows without your hips dropping. | Reverse the rotation and bring your torso back through center, then continue to the left side for one full repetition. | Continue alternating sides for the prescribed number of repetitions, maintaining tension in your obliques throughout.

t: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and feet flat. t: Place a weight plate, squat wedge, or similar stable surface on the floor. Position your heels on the elevation with your toes pointing slightly outward and your feet roughly shoulder-width apart. | Stand tall with your arms extended in front of you at shoulder height for balance, or cross them over your chest. | Brace your core, take a deep breath, and keep your chest up and gaze forward. | Push your hips back slightly, then bend your knees and lower your body in a controlled descent, tracking your knees over your toes. | Continue lowering until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor, or as deep as your mobility allows without your lower back rounding. | Pause briefly at the bottom, maintaining an upright torso and keeping your weight evenly distributed across your feet. | Drive through your heels and the balls of your feet to press the floor away and return to the standing position. | Fully extend your hips and knees at the top without locking out aggressively, then repeat for the desired number of reps.

t: Stand with your feet roughly shoulder-width apart and toes turned out slightly. | Position the bar across the front of your shoulders with the padded yoke resting on your traps and front deltoids. | Grip the handles or keep your hands at your sides — do not pull down on the bar. | Brace your core, take a deep breath into your belly, and tighten your upper back to keep the torso upright. | Initiate the squat by pushing your knees out in line with your toes while simultaneously sitting your hips back and down. | Descend until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor, maintaining an upright torso throughout. | Pause briefly at the bottom, then drive through your full foot to stand back up, keeping your chest tall. | Lock out your hips and knees at the top and exhale before beginning the next rep.

t: Set the safety squat bar in a rack at approximately shoulder height and duck under it so the padded yoke sits across your upper traps, just below the base of your neck. | Grip the forward-facing handles firmly and stand upright to unrack the bar, then take two controlled steps back. | Set your feet shoulder-width apart with toes turned out slightly, brace your core hard, and take a deep breath into your belly. | Push your hips back first, maintaining a neutral or very slightly arched spine, and allow your torso to hinge forward under the bar. | Continue hinging until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor or until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings — whichever limit you reach first. | Hold the bottom position for one count without rounding your lower back or letting your knees collapse inward. | Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to return your torso to upright, exhaling on the way up. | Stand fully tall with hips locked out at the top before beginning the next rep. | After completing all reps, step forward and re-rack the bar under control.

t: Sit on the floor with both legs extended straight in front of you in Dandasana (Staff Pose). Keep your spine tall and your hands flat on the floor beside your hips. | Bend your right knee and draw the right foot flat to the floor, placing it close to your right sitting bone with the shin roughly vertical. | Root both sitting bones evenly into the floor. If your lower back rounds immediately, sit on a folded blanket to tilt the pelvis forward. | On an inhale, lengthen your spine upward. Wrap your right arm around the inside of your right shin, then reach behind your back with your right hand while sweeping your left arm behind you to clasp both hands — or use a strap if the hands do not yet reach. | On an exhale, hinge forward from the hips — not the waist — over the extended left leg, keeping the spine as long as possible rather than rounding. | Allow your torso to descend toward your left thigh. t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, holding a medicine ball at chest height with both hands and your elbows pointing down. | Brace your core and keep your chest up as you step one foot forward into a long stride. | Lower your back knee toward the floor, descending into a full lunge so your front thigh is roughly parallel to the ground. | At the bottom of the lunge, press the medicine ball directly overhead until your arms are fully extended, keeping your torso upright. | Pause briefly with the ball locked out overhead and your front knee tracking over your toes. | Lower the medicine ball back to chest height with control as you begin to rise. | Push through your front heel to return to the starting position, stepping your front foot back beside the other so your feet are hip-width apart again. | Alternate legs for the desired number of reps, or complete all reps on one side before switching.

t: Sit tall on the floor with your legs extended straight in front of you and spread apart to a comfortable V-shape, roughly shoulder-width or slightly wider. | Flex your feet so your toes point toward the ceiling, and press through your heels to keep your legs grounded. | Sit up as tall as possible, lengthening through the crown of your head and keeping your spine neutral. | Extend both arms out to your sides at shoulder height, palms facing down. | Inhale to prepare, then exhale as you rotate your torso to the right, bringing your left hand toward the outside of your right foot in a reaching, 'sawing' motion. | Pulse your left little finger gently past your right pinky toe three times, reaching a little further with each exhale to deepen the stretch through the left waist and obliques. | Inhale as you unwind and return to the upright, centered position with arms extended to the sides. | Exhale and repeat the rotation to the left side, reaching your right hand toward the outside of your left foot. | Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions, then sit tall to finish the set.

t: Stand or sit tall with your arms relaxed at your sides, spine neutral, and feet hip-width apart. | Let your shoulders hang in their natural resting position — this is your starting point. | Inhale and shrug both shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as you can, keeping your neck long and your head still. | Hold the elevated position for one to two seconds, feeling the upper trapezius contract. | Exhale and pull your shoulders down deliberately, drawing the shoulder blades away from your ears and toward your back pockets. | Hold the depressed position for one to two seconds, feeling the lower trapezius and serratus anterior engage. | Return to the neutral resting position in a controlled manner. | Repeat for the target number of repetitions, maintaining a slow, deliberate tempo throughout.

t: Start in a quadruped position with your hands directly under your shoulders and knees under your hips, spine neutral. | Keep your elbows straight and your head in line with your torso throughout the movement. | Inhale to prepare, then exhale and let your shoulder blades slide apart — push the floor away so your upper back rises slightly toward the ceiling (protraction). | Hold the protracted position for one to two seconds, feeling the stretch between the shoulder blades. | Inhale and draw your shoulder blades toward each other, allowing your chest to drop gently toward the floor (retraction). | Hold the retracted position for one to two seconds, feeling the squeeze in the mid-back. | Continue alternating between protraction and retraction in a slow, controlled rhythm for the prescribed number of repetitions.

t: Grip a pull-up bar with both hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, using an overhand (pronated) grip. | Hang at full arm extension — this is the dead-hang starting position. Let your shoulders rise naturally toward your ears and allow your body to relax. | Keep your elbows completely straight and locked throughout the entire movement. This is a scapular drill, not a pull-up. | Exhale and depress your shoulder blades — think of pulling your shoulders away from your ears and driving them straight down toward your hips. | Simultaneously retract your scapulae by squeezing them together slightly, 'packing' your shoulders down and back. | Pause for a full second at the top of the movement. Your body will visibly rise an inch or two without any elbow bend. | Inhale and slowly release, letting your shoulders rise back up to the fully elevated dead-hang position. | Repeat for the target number of reps, maintaining control throughout each rep without swinging or kipping.

This is a scapular drill, not a pull-up. | Exhale and depress your shoulder blades — think of pulling your shoulders away from your ears and driving them straight down toward your hips. | Simultaneously retract your scapulae by squeezing them together slightly, 'packing' your shoulders down and back. | Pause for a full second at the top of the movement. Your body will visibly rise an inch or two without any elbow bend. | Inhale and slowly release, letting your shoulders rise back up to the fully elevated dead-hang position. | Repeat for the target number of reps, maintaining control throughout each rep without swinging or kipping.

t: Grip a pull-up bar with an overhand (pronated) grip slightly wider than shoulder-width, wrapping your thumbs fully around the bar. | Hang at full arm extension with your legs straight or slightly crossed, allowing your shoulder blades to rise naturally into a passive shrug — this is your starting dead-hang position. | Without bending your elbows, depress and retract your shoulder blades: pull them down toward your back pockets and squeeze them gently together. | Your body will rise a few centimeters and your chest will lift slightly — this is the scapular pull. t: Stand with your back, head, and glutes fully against a wall, feet a few inches away from the base and shoulder-width apart. | Press your lower back into the wall as much as possible to reduce the lumbar arch — a slight gap is acceptable, but minimize it. | Raise your arms to a 90/90 position: upper arms out to the sides at shoulder height, elbows bent to 90°, and forearms vertical with the backs of your hands touching the wall. | Brace your core lightly and retract your shoulder blades to establish contact between your entire forearms, wrists, and the backs of your hands and the wall. | Exhale and slowly slide both forearms upward along the wall, straightening your elbows as your arms reach overhead — keep every part of your arms in contact with the wall throughout. | Continue until your arms are fully extended overhead, or until you can no longer maintain wall contact without compensating. | Pause briefly at the top, then inhale and reverse the motion, sliding your arms back down to the starting 90/90 position under control. | Complete the target number of repetitions, maintaining wall contact and scapular control on every rep.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and your core braced. | Step your right foot forward and your left foot back into a split stance, as if you were at the bottom of a lunge — front knee bent to roughly 90°, back knee lowered toward the floor. | Swing your arms back to load for the jump. | Drive explosively through both feet, pressing the floor away to launch yourself into the air. | While airborne, scissor your legs by swinging your left foot forward and your right foot back, simultaneously switching your arm swing to the opposite side. | Land softly with your left foot now forward and your right foot back, absorbing impact through your heel-to-toe and bending both knees to cushion the landing. | Without pausing, immediately load for the next jump and repeat the switch — each landing counts as one rep. | Continue alternating legs for the target number of reps or time.

t: Sit tall on a sturdy chair with your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart, and your back straight away from the backrest. | Raise both arms out to your sides and bend your elbows to 90°, bringing your upper arms parallel to the floor in a goalpost position. | Keep your wrists roughly in line with your elbows and your shoulders pulled slightly back and down — avoid shrugging. | Take a deep breath in, brace your core, and squeeze your chest muscles to drive your elbows toward each other in front of your body. | Continue pressing your elbows together until they meet or nearly meet at chest height, pausing at the peak contraction for one to two seconds. | Slowly reverse the movement, resisting as you open your arms back to the goalpost starting position, maintaining tension through the chest. | Repeat for the desired number of reps, keeping your torso upright and still throughout the set.

nE: Seated Wrist Ulnar Deviator And Flexor Stretch
t: Sit upright on a chair or bench with your feet flat on the floor and your back away from the backrest. | Extend your right arm in front of you at roughly chest height, elbow straight or very slightly soft. | Rotate your palm to face the floor so your wrist is in a neutral, pronated position. | Curl your fingers and wrist downward into flexion, pointing your fingertips toward the floor. | Simultaneously shift your wrist toward the pinky side, adding ulnar deviation to the flexion. | Reach across with your left hand and wrap your fingers gently over the back of your right hand. | Use your left hand to apply light overpressure, deepening both the flexion and the ulnar deviation until you feel a stretch along the thumb side and top of your right forearm. | Hold the stretch for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily, then release slowly. | Repeat on the opposite side.

t: Place a foam roller on the floor and kneel behind it with your hands in front of you in a tabletop or push-up position. | Lower the front of your lower leg onto the foam roller so that it sits just below the knee, contacting the tibialis anterior along the outer shin — not the bony shin bone itself. | Support your body weight through your hands and keep your core lightly braced. | Slowly shift your weight forward to roll the foam roller down toward your ankle, moving a few centimeters at a time. | When you reach a tender or tight spot, pause and hold for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and allowing the pressure to soften the tissue. | Continue rolling from just below the knee down to just above the ankle, spending extra time on any areas that feel particularly tense. | Roll back up toward the knee using the same slow, controlled pace. | Complete 1–2 passes on each leg, then switch sides.

t: Kneel on a padded surface with your knees hip-width apart and your feet anchored firmly under a heavy barbell, the base of a sofa, or held down by a partner. | Extend your hips fully so your torso is upright and your body forms a straight line from knees to head. | Hold your arms close to your chest with your palms facing outward, ready to extend and catch yourself near the bottom of the rep. | Take a breath in, brace your core hard, and squeeze your glutes to lock your hips in place. | Slowly lower your torso toward the floor by extending your knees, using your hamstrings to resist gravity. Aim for a controlled four- to six-second descent. | When you can no longer control the descent with your hamstrings, extend your arms and place your palms on the floor close to your body rather than far in front of you. | Press firmly into the floor with both hands to assist your hamstrings in driving your torso back up to the starting position — use only as much push as necessary. | As your torso rises, actively pull with your hamstrings and shift the effort away from your arms as quickly as possible. | Return fully upright, reset your brace, and repeat for the target number of repetitions.

t: Position yourself beneath a fixed horizontal bar set at hip to waist height — a Smith machine bar, a low pull-up bar, or a sturdy table edge works well. | Lie on your back with your head just inside the bar and your arms extended overhead so both hands can reach it. | Grip the bar with both hands, palms facing up (supinated grip), arms fully extended above your chest. | Release your non-working hand and place it on your working wrist or forearm to provide light, controlled assistance. | Keeping your core braced and your body straight, pull the bar down toward your hips in a wide arc, leading with straight or slightly soft elbows. | Continue the arc until your hands reach your thighs and your lats are fully contracted, allowing your assisting hand to contribute only as much force as necessary. | Slowly reverse the arc, guiding the bar back overhead under control until your arms are fully extended and you feel a stretch across the lats. | Complete all reps on one side, then switch so the other hand takes the primary role.

t: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and your toes pointing slightly outward. | Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to lower into a partial squat, stopping when your thighs are at roughly a 45-degree angle to the floor rather than parallel. | Keep your chest tall, your core braced, and your weight evenly distributed across both feet. | From the semi-squat position, drive explosively through your heels and the balls of your feet to jump straight up. | Extend your hips, knees, and ankles fully at the top of the jump. | Land softly with your knees slightly bent to absorb the impact, returning directly to the semi-squat position. | Maintain a controlled, rhythmic pace, keeping your core engaged throughout each repetition.

t: Sit upright in a chair or on the floor with your feet flat and accessible. | Lift one foot and rest it across the opposite thigh so you can comfortably reach your toes. | Interlace the fingers of one hand between all five toes, weaving each finger into the gaps as far as is comfortable. | Gently squeeze your hand to spread your toes apart, creating separation between each toe. | Hold the spread position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the tissues to release. | While holding, you can slowly circle the ankle in both directions to combine toe separation with ankle mobility. | Release the hand grip and let the toes return to their natural position. | Repeat on the other foot.

t: Sit or stand in a comfortable, upright position with your shoulders relaxed. | Extend one arm in front of you with your palm facing down and your elbow slightly soft. | Spread all five fingers apart as wide as you can, creating as much space between each finger as possible. | Hold the fully spread position for 5–10 seconds, feeling the stretch across the top of your hand and into your forearm. | Relax your fingers back to a neutral position, then repeat the spread 3–5 times on the same hand. | To deepen the stretch, use your opposite hand to gently press each finger outward one at a time. | Switch to the other hand and repeat the same sequence. | Perform 2–3 sets per hand, breathing steadily throughout.

t: Stand facing a smooth wall with your feet hip-width apart and about 15–20 cm away from the wall. | Place both forearms flat against the wall at roughly shoulder height, elbows bent to 90°, with your forearms vertical and hands pointing toward the ceiling. | Gently brace your core and tuck your chin slightly so your neck is long and neutral. | Reach your arms upward by sliding your forearms along the wall, actively pushing your chest away from the wall as you raise your arms. | Continue sliding until your arms are nearly fully extended overhead, keeping both forearms in contact with the wall throughout. | At the top, consciously protract and elevate your shoulder blades — think of pushing the wall away and reaching tall through your fingertips. | Slowly slide your forearms back down to the starting 90° position under control, resisting the urge to let your lower back arch. | Repeat for the desired number of reps, maintaining steady contact between your forearms and the wall on every repetition.

t: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and your feet roughly hip-width apart. Rotate both knees to the left so your left shin is in front of you and your right shin is behind you, each forming a 90-degree angle — this is the 90-90 position. | Place your hands lightly on the floor behind you for initial support, keeping your torso upright. | Press the outer edge of your front shin and the inner edge of your rear shin gently into the floor to feel the hip stretch on both sides. | To switch, lift both knees off the floor simultaneously, rotating your hips so your knees pass through center and drop to the opposite side. | Land with your right shin now in front and your left shin behind, re-establishing the 90-90 position on the other side. | Sit tall, minimize leaning on your hands as your mobility improves, and feel the stretch settle into your hips. | Continue alternating sides in a slow, controlled rhythm for the desired number of repetitions.

t: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, spine neutral, and core lightly braced. | Let both arms hang relaxed at your sides with palms facing your thighs. | Keeping the elbow soft (very slightly bent), begin raising one arm out to the side in the frontal plane. | Rotate the arm so the thumb leads the movement as the arm rises past waist height, allowing the shoulder to open naturally. | Continue lifting the arm in a smooth, controlled arc until it reaches full overhead position or the end of your comfortable range. | Pause briefly at the top to feel the stretch across the anterior deltoid, lateral deltoid, and clavicular pec head. | Slowly lower the arm back down along the same arc, maintaining control throughout the descent. | Complete all reps on one side, then repeat on the opposite arm. | Perform 8–12 slow, deliberate repetitions per side for 2–3 sets.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, core lightly braced, and chest open. Let both arms hang relaxed at your sides. | Raise one arm straight out to the side to roughly shoulder height (90° of abduction) with your palm facing down. | Begin the articulation by slowly sweeping that arm downward and across the front of your body in a smooth arc, leading with the back of your hand. | Continue the arc until your arm crosses the midline of your body as far as your range of motion comfortably allows, feeling a stretch through the lat, pec, teres major, and triceps. | Pause briefly at end range to allow the tissues to lengthen, without forcing the joint. | Reverse the movement under control, sweeping the arm back out to the starting position along the same arc. | Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then switch to the opposite arm. | Keep your torso still throughout — resist the urge to rotate the trunk to compensate for limited shoulder range.

nE: Shoulder Adductor Elevator And Protractor Stretch
t: Stand or sit tall with your spine neutral and your feet hip-width apart if standing. | Raise one arm and reach it across your body at shoulder height, drawing it toward the opposite shoulder. | Use your opposite hand to grasp just above the elbow of the reaching arm and gently pull it closer to your chest. | As you apply the pull, allow your shoulder blade to round forward slightly so the serratus anterior and pectoralis minor are also engaged in the stretch. | Simultaneously let your shoulder shrug upward slightly to load the levator scapulae and upper trapezius portion of the stretch. | Hold the combined position for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the muscles to release with each exhale. | Release slowly, lower the arm, and repeat on the opposite side. | Perform 2 to 3 repetitions per side.

tHe: עמוד או שב זקוף עם עמוד שדרה ניטרלי ורגליים ברוחב האגן בעמידה. | Raise one arm and reach it across your body at shoulder height, drawing it toward the opposite shoulder. | Use your opposite hand to grasp just above the elbow of the reaching arm and gently pull it closer to your chest. | בזמן המשיכה, תן לשכמה להתעגל מעט קדימה כדי שגם המסור הקדמי והחזה הקטן ישתתפו במתיחה. | Simultaneously let your shoulder shrug upward slightly to load the levator scapulae and upper trapezius portion of the stretch. | Hold the combined position for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing steadily and allowing the muscles to release with each exhale. | Release slowly, lower the arm, and repeat on the opposite side. | בצע 2 עד 3 חזרות לכל צד.

nE: Shoulder Adductor Protractor And Elevator Stretch
t: Stand or sit tall with your spine neutral and feet shoulder-width apart. | Raise one arm to approximately shoulder height and draw it horizontally across your chest toward the opposite shoulder (adduction). | Use your opposite forearm or hand to gently press the stretching arm closer to your chest, deepening the adduction. | While holding that position, allow the shoulder of the stretching arm to round forward slightly (protraction) — do not rotate your torso to achieve this. | With the arm still held across your chest, gently shrug that shoulder upward toward your ear (elevation) to add the third component of the stretch. | Hold the combined position — arm across chest, shoulder protracted and elevated — for 20 to 30 seconds. | Breathe steadily throughout; exhale to relax deeper into the stretch on each breath. | Release slowly and lower the arm back to your side. | Repeat on the other side for equal time.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and your arms relaxed at your sides. | Reach both arms behind your back and interlace your fingers, palms facing each other, as low on your back as is comfortable. | Straighten your elbows fully and rotate your palms so they face downward or slightly away from your body. | Inhale to lengthen your spine, then gently squeeze your shoulder blades together and draw them downward away from your ears. | On an exhale, slowly lift your clasped hands away from your lower back, extending your arms backward and upward as far as your shoulder mobility allows without pain. | At the same time, lift your chest forward and upward into a gentle backbend, keeping your chin level and your neck long. | Hold this stretched position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and deeply to allow the muscles to relax further into the stretch. | On an exhale, slowly lower your hands back toward your lower back, release the clasp, and let your arms return to your sides. | Repeat for 2–3 sets, resting briefly between holds.
tRu: Встаньте прямо, поставив ноги на ширине бёдер, руки свободно опущены вдоль тела. | Reach both arms behind your back and interlace your fingers, palms facing each other, as low on your back as is comfortable. | Straighten your elbows fully and rotate your palms so they face downward or slightly away from your body. | Inhale to lengthen your spine, then gently squeeze your shoulder blades together and draw them downward away from your ears. | On an exhale, slowly lift your clasped hands away from your lower back, extending your arms backward and upward as far as your shoulder mobility allows without pain. | Одновременно поднимите грудь вперёд и вверх в мягкий прогиб, удерживая подбородок ровно, а шею длинной. | Hold this stretched position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and deeply to allow the muscles to relax further into the stretch. | On an exhale, slowly lower your hands back toward your lower back, release the clasp, and let your arms return to your sides. | Repeat for 2–3 sets, resting briefly between holds.
tHe: עמוד זקוף עם רגליים ברוחב האגן וידיים רפויות לצדי הגוף. | Reach both arms behind your back and interlace your fingers, palms facing each other, as low on your back as is comfortable. | Straighten your elbows fully and rotate your palms so they face downward or slightly away from your body. | Inhale to lengthen your spine, then gently squeeze your shoulder blades together and draw them downward away from your ears. | On an exhale, slowly lift your clasped hands away from your lower back, extending your arms backward and upward as far as your shoulder mobility allows without pain. | בו זמנית הרם את החזה קדימה ומעלה לקשת גב עדינה, תוך שמירה על סנטר בגובה אחיד וצוואר ארוך. | Hold this stretched position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and deeply to allow the muscles to relax further into the stretch. | On an exhale, slowly lower your hands back toward your lower back, release the clasp, and let your arms return to your sides. | Repeat for 2–3 sets, resting briefly between holds.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your knees bent and feet placed hip-width apart, flat on the floor. | Position your arms alongside your body with palms facing down. | Press your feet firmly into the floor and engage the muscles around your hips and waist. | Exhale and slowly lift your hips off the mat, rolling up through the spine one vertebra at a time. | Continue raising your hips until your body forms a straight diagonal line from your shoulders to your knees. | Hold the top position for the desired duration, keeping your thighs parallel and your chin slightly away from your chest. | Inhale and slowly lower your hips back to the mat, reversing the movement vertebra by vertebra. | Return your hips fully to the starting position and relax before repeating.

t: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart and your arms relaxed at your sides. | Raise both shoulders upward toward your ears, initiating the circular motion. | Roll your shoulders back, squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the movement. | Continue the circle by dropping your shoulders down and back, feeling a stretch across the front of your chest. | Roll your shoulders forward and upward to complete one full circle, keeping the motion smooth and controlled. | Perform the desired number of repetitions in this direction, then reverse the motion to roll your shoulders in the opposite direction. | Finish the set with your shoulders relaxed and your posture upright.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and your arms hanging at your sides. | Relax your shoulders down and back so there is no tension in your neck or upper traps. | Keeping your elbow straight, slowly begin to move one arm backward behind your body, leading with the back of your hand. | Continue moving the arm backward through its comfortable range, feeling a stretch in the lats, chest, and the back of the upper arm. | At the end of your comfortable range, pause for one to two seconds without forcing the joint further. | Slowly return the arm forward to the starting position in a controlled arc. | Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then switch to the other arm. | Keep your torso upright throughout and avoid rotating the trunk to compensate for limited shoulder range.

nE: Shoulder Extensor Adductor And Retractor Stretch
t: Stand tall or sit upright with your feet shoulder-width apart and your spine neutral. | Extend your right arm straight out in front of you at shoulder height, palm facing down. | Bring the right arm horizontally across your chest toward the left shoulder. | Hook your left forearm or hand under the right elbow to support and gently draw the arm closer to your chest. | Keep your right shoulder down and away from your ear — do not let it shrug up. | Hold the stretch for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily and relaxing deeper into the position with each exhale. | Release slowly and return the arm to the starting position. | Repeat on the left side, holding for the same duration. | Perform 2–3 rounds per side as part of your warm-up or cooldown routine.

t: Stand tall or sit upright on a bench with your spine neutral and your feet flat on the floor. | Raise your right arm to the side so your upper arm is parallel to the floor and your elbow is bent to 90°, forearm pointing straight up. | Keep your upper arm fixed and stationary throughout the test — it should not drift forward, backward, or drop. | Slowly rotate your forearm backward and downward, as if trying to lay the back of your hand on a surface behind you. | Stop rotating when you feel resistance, tension, or discomfort — do not force past that point. | Note the angle your forearm makes relative to vertical. A neutral starting position is 0°; full external rotation for most healthy shoulders reaches 90° (forearm horizontal, parallel to the floor). | Return your forearm to vertical and repeat on the left arm. | Compare the range of motion between both sides and record any asymmetry or limitation.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, arms resting at your sides, and your core lightly braced. | Relax the shoulder you are about to move — let it sit in its natural, neutral position before you begin. | Keeping your elbow straight but not locked, begin raising your arm forward with the palm facing down or inward. | Move the arm slowly and smoothly, tracing a straight path upward in front of your body. | Continue lifting until you reach the end of your comfortable range — ideally overhead with the arm alongside your ear. | Pause briefly at the top, allowing the anterior deltoid and upper chest to feel a gentle lengthening. | Lower the arm back down at the same controlled pace, resisting gravity the entire way. | Complete all repetitions on one side before switching, or alternate arms for the prescribed number of reps. | Aim for fluid, continuous motion — treat each repetition as an exploration of your range rather than a race.

t: Stand with your back, head, and hips pressed firmly against a wall, feet roughly 15 to 30 centimetres away from the base. | Begin with your arms at your sides, palms facing forward, elbows straight. | Press the entire length of your spine and the back of your head into the wall and maintain that contact throughout the movement. | Slowly raise both arms forward and upward, keeping the elbows straight and palms facing the ceiling as your arms travel overhead. | Continue lifting until your arms are fully overhead, reaching as high as possible while your back and head remain in contact with the wall. | Hold the end position for one to two seconds, feeling the stretch across the posterior shoulder area and the engagement through the upper back. | Lower your arms back to the starting position in a slow, controlled manner. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining wall contact on every rep.

t: Lie on your back on a firm, flat surface with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor. | Raise your right arm out to the side until it is level with your shoulder — 90° of abduction — and bend your elbow to 90° so your forearm points straight up toward the ceiling. | Allow your upper arm to rest fully on the floor; your elbow should stay in contact with the surface throughout the test. | Keeping your elbow fixed and your upper arm pinned to the floor, slowly rotate your forearm forward and downward toward the floor — this is internal rotation. | Stop when you feel resistance or when your elbow begins to lift off the surface, noting the angle your forearm makes with the floor. | Hold the end-range position for 2–3 seconds to confirm this is your true limit, not muscular guarding. | Return your forearm to the starting vertical position under control. | Repeat the assessment on the left side and compare the range of motion between arms. | Record any asymmetry greater than 10–15° or any reproduction of familiar pain as a positive finding warranting follow-up.

t: Stand or sit tall with your spine neutral and your feet hip-width apart if standing. | Bring your right arm out to the side at shoulder height, elbow bent to 90 degrees so your forearm points straight up toward the ceiling. | Keep your upper arm parallel to the floor and your elbow fixed at shoulder height throughout the movement. | Slowly rotate your forearm downward and backward — externally rotating the upper arm — until your forearm is parallel to the floor or until you reach a comfortable end range. | Pause briefly at the end range, feeling a gentle stretch across the posterior shoulder and rotator cuff. | Slowly reverse the motion, rotating the forearm back up to the starting vertical position in a controlled, deliberate arc. | Perform 8–12 slow, controlled rotations on one side, pausing at the end range of each rep. | Switch to the opposite arm and repeat for the same number of repetitions. | Complete 2–3 sets per side, focusing on smooth movement and increasing range of motion with each repetition.

t: Stand upright in a relaxed, natural posture with your feet hip-width apart and your arms hanging loosely at your sides. | Look straight ahead at a fixed point on the wall or in a mirror at eye level to avoid tilting your head. | Relax your shoulders completely — do not shrug, pull them back, or force them into any particular position. | Have an observer stand directly in front of you, or position yourself in front of a full-length mirror so both shoulders are visible simultaneously. | Observe the height of the bony tip of each shoulder (the acromion) and note whether one side sits higher, lower, or level with the other. | Take a deep breath, relax, and repeat the observation two or three times to confirm the finding is consistent rather than a momentary postural shift. | Record which shoulder appears elevated or depressed, and note whether the difference is subtle or pronounced, to guide any follow-up assessment or corrective work.

t: Stand tall or sit upright with your spine neutral and your feet hip-width apart. | Raise one arm to shoulder height with the elbow bent to 90°, so your forearm points straight up toward the ceiling. | Keeping the upper arm parallel to the floor and the elbow fixed in position, slowly rotate your forearm downward in front of you until it points toward the floor. | Pause at the end range, feeling a gentle stretch across the front of the shoulder and chest. | Slowly return the forearm back to the starting upright position under full control. | Complete all reps on one side before switching to the opposite arm. | Breathe steadily throughout — exhale as you rotate inward, inhale as you return.

t: Stand with both feet hip-width apart and centered on the middle of the band, or loop the band under one foot for a narrower stance. | Grasp one end of the band in each hand and bring your hands up to shoulder height with your palms facing forward and elbows pointed out to the sides. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and maintain a neutral spine — avoid arching your lower back. | Press both hands directly overhead in a straight vertical path until your arms are fully extended without locking the elbows forcefully. | Pause briefly at the top, ensuring the band does not pull you forward or to one side. | Lower your hands in a controlled manner back to shoulder height, resisting the pull of the band on the way down. | Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, keeping tension in the band throughout the entire set.

t: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your arms alongside your body, palms facing down and legs fully extended. | Press your palms and arms firmly into the mat, then engage your core and swing your legs up overhead, bringing your hips off the floor. | Bend your elbows and place your hands on your lower back, fingers pointing upward, to form a supportive shelf for your spine. | Walk your hands higher up your back toward the shoulder blades to straighten your torso as vertical as possible. | Extend your legs straight up toward the ceiling, squeezing your thighs and pointing your toes so your body forms a single vertical line from shoulders to feet. | Keep your weight distributed evenly across both shoulders and your upper back — not your neck — and gaze softly at your toes or the ceiling. | Hold the position for the desired duration while breathing steadily through your nose. | To exit, lower your legs slowly back overhead, release your hands to the mat, and unroll your spine back down to the floor one vertebra at a time.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and your spine in a neutral position. | Reach both arms behind your back and clasp your hands together, interlacing your fingers. | Straighten your arms as much as your shoulder mobility allows, keeping your elbows as extended as possible. | Gently squeeze your shoulder blades together and then press your clasped hands away from your body and slightly downward. | Hold your chest up and avoid rounding your upper back or pushing your head forward. | Breathe deeply and hold the stretch for 20–30 seconds, feeling the pull across the back of your shoulders and upper back. | Release slowly, bring your arms back to your sides, and repeat for the desired number of sets.

t: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and hold one end of a towel in your right hand. | Raise your right arm overhead, bend the elbow so your right hand drops behind your head, and let the towel hang down your back. | Reach your left arm behind your lower back and bend the elbow upward so your left hand can grasp the lower end of the towel. | Gently walk your hands closer together along the towel until you feel a moderate stretch in both shoulders — stop before any pain. | Hold the position for 20–30 seconds, breathing slowly and letting the shoulders relax deeper into the stretch with each exhale. | Release the towel, lower both arms, and shake them out briefly. | Switch sides: raise your left arm overhead and reach your right arm up from below, then repeat the same hold.

t: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart and your core lightly braced. | Bring your right arm across your body at shoulder height, so the hand reaches toward your left shoulder — this is the starting position. | Keep a slight bend in the elbow throughout the movement to reduce joint stress. | Slowly sweep the arm horizontally outward (transverse abduction) until it points directly to your right side or slightly behind it. | Feel the stretch deepen in the rear deltoid and the rotator cuff muscles (infraspinatus and teres minor) as the arm moves away from the body. | Pause briefly at the end range, then return the arm back across the body to the starting position in a controlled arc. | Complete the desired number of repetitions on the right side, then switch arms and repeat. | Breathe steadily throughout — exhale as the arm sweeps outward, inhale as it returns across the body.

t: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, core lightly braced, and your spine in a neutral position. | Extend your working arm out to your side at shoulder height, palm facing forward or down, so it is roughly parallel to the floor. | Begin the movement by driving your arm forward and across your body in a smooth horizontal arc, keeping it at shoulder height throughout. | Continue sweeping the arm past the midline of your chest until it reaches the opposite side of your body — as far as your shoulder mobility comfortably allows. | Pause briefly at the end range to let the pectoralis major fully shorten. | Reverse the arc in a controlled manner, returning the arm back out to the starting position at your side. | Allow a small, natural rotation of the torso if your mobility requires it, but keep the movement led by the shoulder rather than the trunk. | Complete all reps on one side, then repeat with the opposite arm. | Perform 10–15 smooth repetitions per side, treating each swing as an active articulation rather than a ballistic throw.

t: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, or sit upright on a bench with a neutral spine. | Extend one arm straight out in front of you at shoulder height, parallel to the floor, with the palm facing inward or downward. | Keeping the arm level and the elbow long, begin sweeping it slowly outward and backward in a wide horizontal arc. | Continue the arc until the arm is as far behind your torso as your comfortable range of motion allows. | Pause briefly at end range and notice the stretch across the posterior shoulder, outer back, and upper arm. | Slowly reverse the motion, sweeping the arm back through the same arc to the starting position in front of you. | Maintain a steady, rhythmic pace — neither rushing the swing nor holding the stretch for an extended count — to keep the movement articular. | Complete all reps on one side, then switch arms and repeat.

t: Lie on your side on the floor with your legs stacked and your body in a straight line from head to feet. | Extend your bottom arm along the floor above your head, palm facing down, to support and stabilize your position. | Place your top hand lightly on the floor in front of your chest for initial balance. | Take a deep breath in to prepare. | As you exhale, reach your top arm straight overhead, extending it fully alongside your bottom arm so both arms are parallel and pointing in the same direction. | Keep your hips stacked and lengthen through your entire top side, feeling the stretch run from your hip up through your latissimus dorsi. | Hold the stretched position for 20–30 seconds, breathing steadily and relaxing deeper into the stretch with each exhale. | Return your top arm to the starting position in front of your chest, then roll onto your other side. | Repeat the stretch on the opposite side for the same duration.

t: Lie on your side on a flat surface with your body in a straight line. t: Set up in a high plank with your hands directly under your shoulders, arms fully extended, and your body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Spread your fingers slightly and press firmly through your palms to stabilize your wrists and shoulders. | Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and keep your hips level — they should not rise or sag. | Drive your right knee out to the right side toward your right elbow, keeping your foot close to the floor and your hips square. | Return your right foot to the starting position with control before initiating the next rep. | Drive your left knee out to the left side toward your left elbow using the same controlled lateral path. | Return your left foot to the starting position to complete one full rep. | Continue alternating sides at a steady pace, breathing rhythmically and maintaining your plank alignment throughout the set.

t: Lie on your side on a flat surface. Stack your feet on top of each other and place your bottom forearm on the floor with your elbow directly beneath your shoulder. | WRONG — Let your hips sag toward the floor so your body forms a downward curve. Notice how this collapses the waist and removes tension from the lateral core. This is the position to avoid. | WRONG (alternative) — Raise your hips too high so your body forms an inverted V (piked). This also misaligns the spine and shifts load away from the target area. | RIGHT — Brace your core and lift your hips off the floor until your body forms a single straight line from your head through your hips to your feet. | Keep your top hand on your hip or extend it toward the ceiling to help with balance. Your neck should remain neutral, aligned with your spine. | Press your bottom forearm into the floor to create a stable base, and squeeze your glutes and lateral core to maintain the rigid plank position. | Hold the correct position for the prescribed duration, breathing steadily. Resist any tendency for the hips to drift down or spike upward. | Lower your hips back to the floor with control to complete the hold, then switch sides.
